title: Did I just snap my sh*t up? (an injury assessment guide & pain psychology discussion)
summary: NH explains that injuries come from pressure combined with fatigue and can be controlled, then argues that pain is an unreliable messenger amplified by fear and nocebo. He gives two six-level guides, one for the moment of a possible injury and one for the aftermath, to decide calmly whether you are actually hurt, with function over sensation as the rule.
claims: Most of the time when lifters think they are injured it is nothing, and taking an unnecessary break actively hurts them
An injury is pressure exceeding what the tissue can handle; pressure itself is necessary because bodybuilding is controlled destruction of muscle fibres that then repair
Muscle belly tears are rare; most lifting injuries involve tendons, and while muscle always heals, a snapped tendon needs surgery
Always choose the form that puts the most pressure on the muscle; training the tendon directly is obsolete for hypertrophy because training the muscle trains the tendon
Injury risk depends on pressure and fatigue together: 50% of max is baby weight, but 5 reps at 80% to failure every day raises the risk daily because fatigue builds while load stays the same
The idea that injuries just happen is lazy fatalism that removes your responsibility and your ability to control them
He has not had even a slight injury for two and a half years because he controls every variable of his training
The goal of managing fatigue and pressure is that any injury that does happen only takes you out for a day or two
Pain cannot be quantified or matched to a degree of damage; it is a messenger that does not always tell the truth
Your brain and body are cowards focused on survival, so they send pain signals for things that mean nothing
Study: blindfolded subjects told they would be shocked rated pain even on trials when no shock was given, because the brain anticipated it
Nocebo is the reverse of placebo: fear fed by injury horror stories can create pain, which convinces you that you are injured and leads you to stop training
False-alarm test: after squats or deadlifts, dead hang and consciously relax your core and glutes and you will feel severe lower back pain that disappears after a few steps of walking
Thinking about pain makes it grow; many lower back injuries are minor pain that gets worse through obsession and inactivity
Do not ignore pain; the pseudoscience claiming all pain is imaginary is reductionist, because pain is a trick to be understood, not an illusion
Pain and damage are separate: pulling out a healthy nail is agonising but does not impair function, and bumping your elbow hurts without damaging the tendon
Muscles have relatively few nerve endings because the body knows they recover well; tendons are much more sensitive because damage to them does not repair

Occurrence level 0 (noise only) and level 1 (pain during a rep) mean nothing: do one more rep, and if the pain stays, stop, walk two minutes without focusing on it and do another set; 99% of the time it is gone
Occurrence level 2 (pain that lasts all workout) is often a small strain, a nocebo or a burst blood vessel; push through or go home to be conservative
Occurrence level 3 (feeling something shift, no pain): do another set; if the sensation is gone, it was nothing
Occurrence level 4 (felt shift plus pain): walk around, and if the pain is still there you are likely injured
Occurrence level 5 (shift, pain and an audible snap) is an injury; level 6 (structural failure during the lift) is a freak accident that is entirely avoidable by managing loads, fatigue and pressure
Experiment: a man told he had a degenerative illness causing phantom arm pain reported escalating pain until he begged for painkillers, though nothing was wrong
Aftermath level 0 is soreness and means nothing; level 1 (pain only when lifting heavy) calls for a different angle or lighter load that day, not stopping
Aftermath level 2 (pain lifting any weight): change the movement or range of motion and keep moving
Aftermath level 3 (pain when walking or moving) usually means injury, often tendinitis from poor recovery; he had crippling tendinitis for years and is now cured
Aftermath level 4 (pain to the touch, not bruises), level 5 (pain at rest, especially pain that wakes you) and level 6 (cannot move) point to real structural damage
The more you respond to small pains, the more your body will send them; assess and push small pains aside so you can recognise a real injury
Put function over sensation: if function shows the body is intact, the sensation does not matter
exercises: relax core and glutes on purpose
shows how harmless positions can create alarming lower back pain
